land.text: the county of Aragon around Jaca: 'the county of Aragon fell to Ramiro with the title of baiulus or steward' on the division of Sancho III's realm in 1035

predecessors.note: The infobox names the County of Aragon as predecessor; the County of Aragon dossier ended in 922, when its counts' dynasty ended and it was absorbed by Pamplona. Cliopatria's 1015-1027 row for this state is a copy of the Pallars Sobirà shape (ledger of keyframes).

land.text: the Kingdom of Aragon at its 1152-1168 shape (Zaragoza, Huesca and Teruel country); infobox 'Status: Independent kingdom (1035-1162); Kingdom of the Crown of Aragon (1162-1707)'; 'Successor: Crown of Aragon (1162)'

successors.note: The Crown of Aragon dossier starts in 1162 and asks this one to end in 1162. The Petronilla page has the wedding in August 1150 and the Kingdom page says the Crown was created in 1150.

land.text: Navarre, separated in 1134: 'After Alfonso the Battler died childless in 1134, different rulers were chosen for Navarre and Aragon'

successors.note: A split during the life, not at its end (ledger 1134).

capitals.name: Jaca
capitals.note: Infobox: Jaca (1035-1096); the capital moved to Huesca in 1096.

capitals.name: Huesca
capitals.note: Infobox: Huesca (1096-1118). The Peter I page ties the transfer to his second marriage at Huesca on 16 August 1097 ('the transferral of the capital of Aragon from Jaca to the larger city of Huesca') and gives no separate year; the Kingdom page's 1096 is kept.

rulers.name: Ramiro I
rulers.title: baiulus, de facto king
rulers.note: Received the county of Aragon in 1035; 'the first de facto king of Aragon, though he never used the title'; died 8 May 1063 at Graus.

rulers.name: Sancho Ramírez
rulers.title: King of the Aragonese and Pamplonese
rulers.note: King of Aragon 1063-1094 and King of Pamplona from 1076; died 4 June 1094 at Huesca.

rulers.name: Peter I
rulers.title: king
rulers.note: 'Peter succeeded to the whole of his father's kingdom on the latter's death while besieging Huesca in 1094' and 'He reigned until his death in 1104' (the page's footnote gives 27, 28 or 29 September); Alfonso I follows in 1104.

rulers.name: Alfonso I the Battler
rulers.note: 'King of Aragon and Navarre from 1104 until his death in 1134' (7 September); also styled Emperor of Spain from 1109.

rulers.name: Ramiro II
rulers.note: Chosen by the Aragonese; 'At El Castellar on 13 November 1137, Ramiro abdicated'.

rulers.name: Petronilla (with Ramon Berenguer IV as princeps)
rulers.title: queen
rulers.note: Betrothed 11 August 1137 to Ramon Berenguer IV, who ruled 'using the title Prince of the Aragonese'; wedding August 1150; she abdicated to Alfonso II on 18 June (or July) 1164, after the dossier's end.

correction.text: the county of Aragon around Jaca; before 1035 it belongs to the Kingdom of Pamplona

keyframe_review.note: 3,039 km2 for 1015-1027 is the Pallars Sobirà shape (12 cells, all inside Cliopatria's County of Pallars Sobirà of 1046) and not Aragon; the kingdom was established in 1035 ('Established: 1035, as an independent kingdom (from the County of Aragon)') and before that Aragon was a county around Jaca inside the Kingdom of Pamplona. Use the Jaca county shape for 1035 and nothing before it in this dossier. The infobox states no area.

correction.text: the county of Aragon around Jaca without the Sangüesa area; drawn 1035-1042

keyframe_review.note: 2,490 km2 (10 cells) as Cliopatria draws it; drawn here as 8 cells for 1035-1042. The county of Aragon around Jaca, Ramiro I's share in 1035. Two cells at Sangüesa (42.48 N 1.38 W, 42.50 N 1.18 W) are cut out, because Sangüesa passes to Ramiro only after the war with García ('Ramiro was defeated at Tafalla but still gained territory, including Sangüesa'; the page puts the war 'from 1036 to 1043'); ledger 1043 adds them back. Sobrarbe and Ribagorza are annexed in 1043 ('In 1043, apparently with the approval of García, he annexed Sobrarbe and Ribagorza').

correction.text: the 1046 shape without the cells round Graus, Barbastro and east of Huesca (42.09-42.25 N, 0.5 E to 0.2 W), which Aragon takes only in 1083, 1096 and 1100; drawn 1043-1075

keyframe_review.note: 10,121 km2 (40 cells) as Cliopatria draws it; drawn here as 33 cells for 1043-1075: the county, Sobrarbe, Ribagorza and the Sangüesa area (Cliopatria's 1040 shape already holds the Sangüesa cells). Seven cells are cut: (42.09 N, 0.11 E) at Barbastro, (42.23 N, 0.18 E) and (42.25 N, 0.37 E) at Graus, (42.11 N, 0.30 E), (42.13 N, 0.50 E), (42.21 N, 0.02 W) and (42.19 N, 0.21 W), because Ramiro 'died at the Battle of Graus in 1063 while trying to take the city' and the towns come only in 1083 (Graus), 1096 (Huesca, the cell east of it) and 1100 (Barbastro). One cell of the 1040 shape (42.79 N, 1.04 W) is absent from Cliopatria's 1046 shape; not drawn as a loss.

correction.text: the 1085 shape without the Huesca cell (42.17 N, 0.41 W) and the Graus-Barbastro cells; drawn 1076-1082

keyframe_review.note: 18,573 km2 (76 cells) as Cliopatria draws it; drawn here as 68 cells for 1076-1082: the 1046 shape plus 35 cells, 28 of them in Navarre ('King of Aragon from 1063 until 1094 and King of Pamplona from 1076'; 'This changed in 1076, when Sancho IV of Navarre was murdered by his own siblings'), so the larger shape is drawn from 1076, nine years before Cliopatria. The Huesca cell (42.17 N, 0.41 W) is cut: Sancho Ramírez 'perished in 1094 at the battle of Huesca' and the city fell in November 1096 (ledger 1096); the seven Graus-Barbastro cells are cut as in the 1046 keyframe.

correction.text: the 1085 shape without the Huesca cell and the Barbastro cells, with Graus; 'In 1083, they took Graus'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1083-1088 (71 cells): the 1076 shape plus the three Graus cells ('In 1083, they took Graus', Lérida page; Sancho Ramírez page: 'Graus in 1083'). Barbastro (taken for good in 1100) and Huesca (1096) are still outside.

correction.text: the 1083 shape with Monzón, Estada and Almenar; 'Monzón in 1089'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1089-1095 (74 cells): the 1083 shape plus the three Monzón cells (41.96 N 0.23 E and neighbours), which Cliopatria draws only from its 1111 shape. 'Sancho conquered ... Monzón in 1089' (the Peter I page: 'Monzón on 24 June 1089'); the Lérida page adds Estada and Almenar 'between 1087 and 1093'.

21,407 km2 (86 cells) as Cliopatria draws it; drawn here as 86 cells for 1096-1099 (the Barbastro cells are cut, Monzón is added). The ten cells it gains over the 1085 shape lie at 42.0-42.4 N, 0.28-1.05 W, on the Huesca plain towards Ayerbe and Almudévar: they are the conquest of Huesca, not the 1100 Barbastro capture. 'The Battle of Alcoraz took place on 15 November 1096'; the siege of Huesca ran 'nearly two and a half years until in November 1096', and 'Less than two weeks later, Huesca surrendered'. The Peter I page puts both in 1095 (Huesca on 27 November); the Alcoraz page, the Kingdom page (capital moved 1096) and the Zaragoza dossier (1096-11) agree on 1096.

correction.text: the 1089 shape with Huesca and the plain west of it, as Cliopatria's 1099 shape draws it, without the Barbastro cells; drawn 1096-1099
the 1096 shape with Barbastro, Sariñena, Pomar de Cinca and Albalate de Cinca; '1100-1101: Aragonese capture Barbastro, Sariñena, Pomar de Cinca, and Albalate de Cinca'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1100-1104 (91 cells): the 1096 shape plus five cells round Barbastro (42.09 N 0.11 E and neighbours; three of them are in Cliopatria's 1046 shape and were cut from 1043 to 1099, two are new in its 1111 shape). 'Barbastro fell in 1100' (Peter I page). Cliopatria's 1111 shape does not reach Sariñena, Pomar or Albalate (three cells at 41.67-41.80 N are only in its 1126 shape), so those towns are named but not drawn.

correction.text: the 1100 shape with Ejea and Tauste and the Cinco Villas country round them; 'In 1105, he conquered Ejea and Tauste and refortified Castellar and Juslibol'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1105-1106 (101 cells): the 1100 shape plus ten cells in the Ebro valley west of Huesca (41.8-42.4 N, 0.9-1.5 W), which Cliopatria draws in its 1111 shape. The page names Ejea and Tauste in 1105 and no other town there; the other cells are Cliopatria's. 'In 1106, he defeated Ahmad II al-Musta'in of Zaragoza at Valtierra'.

correction.text: the 1105 shape with Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera; 'In 1107, he took Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1107-1110 (105 cells): the 1105 shape plus four cells in La Litera (41.84 N 0.36 E, 41.86 N 0.55 E, 41.98 N 0.43 E, 42.0 N 0.62 E). The shape equals Cliopatria's 1111 shape plus one cell (42.0 N 0.67 W).

25,654 km2 (104 cells) as Cliopatria draws it; drawn here as 105 cells for 1111-1117. Cliopatria's shape grows by 19 cells over its 1099 shape; the ledger now explains them: Barbastro, Monzón and the Cinca (1089, 1100), Ejea, Tauste and the Cinco Villas (1105), La Litera (1107). One cell of the 1099 shape (42.0 N 0.67 W, near Almudévar) is missing from Cliopatria's 1111 shape and back in its 1126 shape; it is kept, no page dates a loss. 'King of Aragon and Navarre from 1104 until his death in 1134'. The Ebro conquests (Zaragoza 18 December 1118, Soria 1119, Calatayud and Daroca 1120) are in the 1118 keyframe.

correction.text: Aragon and Navarre under Alfonso I, as Cliopatria draws 1111 plus the one cell of its 1099 shape that it drops; drawn 1111-1117
Aragon and Navarre with the Ebro valley from Zaragoza to Calatayud and Daroca, the Soria region and the Tudela area

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1118-1125: the 1111 shape plus the Ebro valley (Zaragoza, 'The city fell on 18 December' 1118; 'When Calatayud fell, he took Bubierca, Alhama de Aragón, Ariza, and Daroca (1120)'), the Soria region ('In 1119 he retook several towns' and 'populated the region of Soria') and Tudela (25 February 1119, es.wikipedia Tudela). Zaragoza and Soria provinces stand for the page's places; the Tudela disc adds five cells Cliopatria's 1111 shape lacks. The step carries the 1118-1120 conquests as one keyframe, drawn from 1118 although Tudela and Soria fall in 1119 and Calatayud and Daroca in 1120.

100,638 km2 (399 cells): Aragon, Navarre and the Castilian possessions (Burgos, Soria, La Rioja, Álava, Guadalajara, Teruel). Alfonso 'styled himself King and Emperor of Castile, Toledo, Aragón, Pamplona, Sobrarbe, and Ribagorza'; 'In 1127, he reconquered Longares, but simultaneously lost all his Castilian possessions to Alfonso VII'. The infobox states no area. Drawn for 1126 only.

correction.text: Aragon and Navarre under Alfonso I after the loss of the Castilian possessions to Alfonso VII

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1127-1133: the 1126 shape without the Castilian possessions (160 cells, the part of the 1126 shape outside both the 1139 Aragon and the 1139 Navarre shapes); 'He confirmed a treaty with Castile the next year (1128) with the Peace of Támara', which set the boundary between the two realms.

37,822 km2 (152 cells): Aragon without Navarre. 'After Alfonso the Battler died childless in 1134, different rulers were chosen for Navarre and Aragon' (Alfonso died in September 1134), so the shape is drawn from 1134 instead of 1139.

37,750 km2 (one cell fewer): Aragon under Ramon Berenguer IV as princeps (1137) and Petronilla; infobox 'Independent kingdom (1035-1162)', Crown 'created in 1150' with the union. Drawn to 1162, when the Crown of Aragon dossier takes the land over (Cliopatria keeps the kingdom's row to 1168).

region.text: the county of Aragon around Jaca

ledger.note: 1035: Ramiro I receives Aragon on his father's death. 'On the death of Sancho III of Navarre in 1035, the Kingdom of Navarre was divided into three parts'; 'the county of Aragon fell to Ramiro with the title of baiulus or steward'; infobox 'Established: 1035, as an independent kingdom'. Ramiro won independence from his brother García Sánchez III of Navarre (undated).

region.text: Sobrarbe and Ribagorza (Cliopatria's 1046 shape over the 1040 shape, without the seven cells round Graus, Barbastro and east of Huesca)

ledger.note: 1043: Ramiro annexes Sobrarbe and Ribagorza. 'In 1043, apparently with the approval of García, he annexed Sobrarbe and Ribagorza', the lands his brother Gonzalo had inherited; the es.wikipedia page has both 'a partir de 1043' and, in its introduction, 'por muerte de su medio hermano Gonzalo en 1045' (the County of Ribagorza dossier ends in 1045). The region leaves out the cells round Graus (taken 1083), Barbastro (1100) and east of Huesca (1096), which Cliopatria's 1046 shape draws too early.

region.text: Sangüesa

ledger.note: 1043 at the latest: Sangüesa passes to Ramiro. After the war with García of Navarre 'Ramiro was defeated at Tafalla but still gained territory, including Sangüesa'; the page puts the war 'from 1036 to 1043' and gives no year for Tafalla, so 1043 is the end of the range (a bridge). The es.wikipedia page dates the war 'probablemente en la primavera o el verano del 1043', Tafalla 'muy pronto' after it, a reconciliation in 1044, but also 'el castillo de Sangüesa' in the alliance with Sancho Garcés IV of 'probablemente octubre del 1057' and Ramiro reigning 'desde Vadoluengo (término de Sangüesa) hasta Ribagorza' in 1049; the pages disagree on when the town came. The two Sangüesa cells (42.48 N 1.38 W, 42.50 N 1.18 W) are in Cliopatria's 1040 shape and are cut from 1035-1042.

region.text: Barbastro

ledger.note: 1064 (August): a Christian army takes Barbastro. The infobox dates the crusade to August 1064; the city 'was besieged for forty days until it surrendered'; 'The leader of the Spaniards was Sancho Ramírez, King of Aragón and Navarre'; 'Armengol III of Urgel, the brother-in-law of King Sancho Ramírez, was entrusted with the government of the city'. The page does not say Aragon kept it, so it is a contest, not a gain.

region.text: Barbastro

ledger.note: 17 April 1065: the Muslims retake Barbastro. 'On 17 April 1065, after roughly ten months of occupation' the city was retaken ('the Moors easily retook the city'); the page does not name the force. Barbastro is taken again only in 1100.

region.text: the Kingdom of Pamplona's lands, mostly Navarre, without the Huesca cell

ledger.note: 1076: Sancho Ramírez becomes King of Pamplona. 'King of Aragon from 1063 until 1094 and King of Pamplona from 1076'; 'This changed in 1076, when Sancho IV of Navarre was murdered by his own siblings'; the page says the crisis 'was resolved by partition' and that Sancho 'ceded previously contested western provinces of the kingdom to Alfonso' (undated). The land is Navarre, as Cliopatria's 1085 shape (35 cells) without its Huesca cell (42.17 N, 0.41 W): 'He perished in 1094 at the battle of Huesca', and the city falls in 1096.

region.text: Graus

ledger.note: 1083: Graus is taken. 'In 1083, they took Graus' (Sancho Ramírez and his son Peter, in the Lérida page's account of the taifa of Lérida); the Sancho Ramírez page: 'Sancho conquered Barbastro in 1064, Graus in 1083, and Monzón in 1089'. The three Graus cells are in Cliopatria's 1046 shape and are drawn here only from 1083. Ramiro I had died 'at the Battle of Graus in 1063 while trying to take the city'. Barbastro in 1064 is the contest of 1064-1065 above.

region.text: Monzón (with Estada and Almenar, per the Lérida page)

ledger.note: 1089: Monzón is conquered. 'Sancho conquered ... Monzón in 1089' (Sancho Ramírez page; the Peter I page has 'Monzón on 24 June 1089'); the Lérida page has 'between 1087 and 1093, Peter took Estada, Monzón and Almenar' from the taifa of Lérida. The three cells are Cliopatria's only from its 1111 shape; drawn here from 1089.

region.text: Huesca and the plain west of it

ledger.note: 1096 (end of November): Peter I takes Huesca. 'The Battle of Alcoraz took place on 15 November 1096'; the siege 'continued for nearly two and a half years until in November 1096'; 'Less than two weeks later, Huesca surrendered.' The Zaragoza taifa's relief army under 'Al-Musta'in II' was beaten. The Peter I page puts the battle in 1095 and the surrender on 27 November 1095; the Alcoraz page, the Kingdom page (capital moved 1096) and the Zaragoza dossier (1096-11) have 1096. The region is the Huesca cell, the cell east of it and the ten cells Cliopatria's 1099 shape adds over its 1085 shape (the Huesca plain towards Ayerbe and Almudévar), twelve cells.

1096: the capital moves from Jaca to Huesca. 'the capital city moved from Jaca to Huesca (1096), and later to Zaragoza (1118)'; Sancho Ramírez had 'perished in 1094 at the battle of Huesca' and the city surrendered at the end of November 1096 (month read from that surrender; the Kingdom page gives only the year). The Peter I page ties the transfer to his marriage at Huesca on 16 August 1097.

region.text: Barbastro and the Cinca, without Graus, Huesca, Monzón and La Litera

ledger.note: 1100: the Aragonese take Barbastro and the Cinca. '1100-1101: Aragonese capture Barbastro, Sariñena, Pomar de Cinca, and Albalate de Cinca' (Lérida page); 'Barbastro fell in 1100' (Peter I page). The region is the 35 km disc round Barbastro without Graus, Huesca, Monzón and La Litera, limited to Cliopatria's 1111 shape: five cells, three of them in its 1046 shape (cut from 1043 to 1099) and two new. It is not the ten-cell growth of Cliopatria's 1099 shape, which lies west of Huesca (the 1096 conquest). Sariñena, Pomar and Albalate lie south of the 1111 shape and are not drawn.

region.text: Ejea and Tauste, with the Cinco Villas country round them

ledger.note: 1105: Alfonso I takes Ejea and Tauste. 'In 1105, he conquered Ejea and Tauste and refortified Castellar and Juslibol.' The page names no holder; the Zaragoza taifa (the Hudid Ahmad II al-Musta'in, beaten at Valtierra in 1106) held the Ebro valley until the Almoravids took it in May 1110. The year is the page's; the ten cells are those Cliopatria's 1111 shape adds in the Cinco Villas and the Ebro valley west of Huesca, the land round Ejea and Tauste.

region.text: Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera, with the land round them

ledger.note: 1107: Alfonso I takes La Litera. 'In 1107, he took Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera.' The page names no holder; the Lérida dossier has the taifa of Lérida ending in 1102 and the Zaragoza dossier has the Hudids of Zaragoza until 1110, so the Zaragoza taifa is read as the holder. Four cells, the Litera and the land east of it in Cliopatria's 1111 shape.

region.text: the city of Zaragoza, the Azuda occupied

ledger.note: 18 December 1118: Alfonso I takes Zaragoza. 'In 1118, the Council of Toulouse declared a crusade to assist in the conquest of Zaragoza'; 'The city fell on 18 December'. The Almoravid dossier of this group has the loss at the same date.

region.text: the region of Soria

ledger.counterpart: holders of the Soria towns (the page names none)
ledger.note: 1119: Alfonso I retakes towns and populates Soria. 'In 1119 he retook several towns, and he populated the region of Soria'; the page names no holder.

region.text: Tudela and the country round it

ledger.note: 25 February 1119: Alfonso I takes Tudela. 'reconquistada definitivamente por el rey Alfonso I el Batallador el 25 de febrero de 1119', 'poco después de la capitulación musulmana de Zaragoza el 18 de diciembre de 1118' (es.wikipedia Tudela). The page does not name the holder; the Almoravids held the Zaragoza taifa from May 1110 (as for Calatayud in 1120). The Alfonso I page lists Tudela among the conquests without a year. The disc is drawn from the 1118 keyframe.

region.text: Calatayud, Bubierca, Alhama de Aragón, Ariza and Daroca

ledger.note: 1120: Calatayud falls and Daroca with it. 'When Calatayud fell, he took Bubierca, Alhama de Aragón, Ariza, and Daroca (1120)'; the page names no holder (the Almoravids held Zaragoza from 1110 in the Almoravid dossier).

region.text: the Castilian possessions and the western Navarre

ledger.note: The Castilian possessions of Alfonso I in Cliopatria's 1126 shape. The page says he took the title Emperor of Spain by his 1109 marriage to Urraca and 'clung to his liaison with Urraca until 1114', and that in 1127 he lost 'all his Castilian possessions'; it dates no acquisition, so 1126 is the shape's year (bridge). Includes Burgos, La Rioja, the Basque provinces, Guadalajara and Teruel. The Urraca page adds: the marriage in October or November 1109 at Monzón, in December 1109 Urraca granted him her whole land, in fall 1112 'Alfonso occupied a significant portion of Castile' and the marriage was annulled; it names no town and no year for the end of that occupation, so the acquisition (1109-1112) and its extent stay unsettled and 1126 is still the bridge.

region.text: all his Castilian possessions

ledger.note: 1127: Alfonso I loses Castile. 'In 1127, he reconquered Longares, but simultaneously lost all his Castilian possessions to Alfonso VII'; 'He confirmed a treaty with Castile the next year (1128) with the Peace of Támara', setting the boundary.

region.text: Navarre

ledger.note: 1134: Navarre separates from Aragon. 'After Alfonso the Battler died childless in 1134, different rulers were chosen for Navarre and Aragon' (the Alfonso I page: died 7 September 1134 after Fraga; Navarrese lords chose García Ramírez, Aragonese Ramiro II).

13 November 1137: Ramiro II abdicates; Ramon Berenguer IV rules Aragon. 'At El Castellar on 13 November 1137, Ramiro abdicated'; Petronilla was betrothed on 11 August 1137 and 'Ramon Berenger ruled the kingdom using the title of Prince of the Aragonese'. Same state, House of Barcelona in place of the Jiménez; the wedding followed in August 1150.

region.text: Tauste, which belonged to Aragon

ledger.note: 1146: García Ramírez of Navarre occupies Tauste. 'In 1146, he occupied Tauste, which belonged to Aragon' (García Ramírez page); the Navarre dossier of this group records the same contest.

region.text: Tauste

ledger.note: 1146: Alfonso VII mediates. 'Alfonso VII intervened to mediate a peace between the two kingdoms'; the page gives no terms and does not say who kept Tauste, so no shape change is drawn (Tauste lies in the 1111 shape).

region.text: the Kingdom of Aragon, united with the County of Barcelona

ledger.note: 1162: the Kingdom of Aragon enters the Crown of Aragon. Infobox 'Independent kingdom (1035-1162); Kingdom of the Crown of Aragon (1162-1707)', 'Successor: Crown of Aragon (1162)'; the text says the Crown was 'created in 1150 with the dynastic union resulting from the marriage of the Queen of Aragon, Petronilla'.

wars.name: Ramiro I's war with García Sánchez III of Navarre
wars.outcome: Ramiro was defeated at Tafalla but gained territory, including Sangüesa.
wars.note: The page dates the conflict 'from 1036 to 1043'; Tafalla has no year.

wars.name: Battle of Graus
wars.outcome: Ramiro I died on 8 May 1063 at Graus 'while trying to take the city'; Graus was conquered by his son in 1083.
wars.note: The Ramiro I page does not name the Muslim defenders.

wars.name: Crusade of Barbastro
wars.outcome: A Christian army, 'the largest component was Aquitainian', took Barbastro after a forty-day siege in August 1064 and Armengol III of Urgel was 'entrusted with the government of the city'; the Muslims retook it on 17 April 1065.
wars.note: The Sancho Ramírez page: 'Sancho conquered Barbastro in 1064'. The Siege page puts the city in the taifa of Lérida and names no force for the 1065 recapture; Aragon does not keep it.

wars.name: Siege of Huesca and Battle of Alcoraz
wars.outcome: Sancho Ramírez began the siege in 1094 and died before the city; Peter I beat the relief army of Al-Musta'in II of Zaragoza at Alcoraz on 15 November 1096 and Huesca surrendered less than two weeks later.
wars.note: The Peter I page puts Alcoraz in 1095 and the fall of Huesca on 27 November 1095; the Alcoraz page, with a siege of 'nearly two and a half years' from 1094, gives November 1096.

wars.name: Aragonese conquest of the Cinca
wars.outcome: Barbastro, Sariñena, Pomar de Cinca and Albalate de Cinca were captured ('1100-1101'; 'Barbastro fell in 1100', Peter I page).
wars.note: Cliopatria's 1111 shape reaches Barbastro and Monzón but not Sariñena, Pomar or Albalate (see keyframe 1100).

wars.name: Alfonso I's first campaigns against Zaragoza

zones.text: Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera

wars.outcome: Ejea and Tauste conquered in 1105; Ahmad II al-Musta'in of Zaragoza defeated at Valtierra in 1106; Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera taken in 1107.
wars.note: The page names no holder for the towns and no capture of Zaragoza before 1118.

wars.name: Conquest of Zaragoza and the Ebro valley
wars.outcome: Zaragoza fell on 18 December 1118; Calatayud and Daroca in 1120 after the Battle of Cutanda (1120), where Alfonso defeated a Muslim army 'intent on reconquering his new capital'.

wars.name: Alfonso I's Castilian war
wars.outcome: Alfonso VII took all of Alfonso I's Castilian possessions in 1127; the Peace of Támara (1128) set the boundary between the realms.
wars.note: The page dates no campaign before 1127; the 1126 start is the shape's.

wars.name: Battle of Fraga
wars.outcome: Alfonso's last campaigns, against Mequinenza (1133) and Fraga (1134), ended in an unsuccessful battle; he died in September 1134.
wars.note: The page gives no capture of either town.

wars.name: Navarrese-Aragonese incident at Tauste
wars.outcome: García Ramírez 'occupied Tauste, which belonged to Aragon'; 'Alfonso VII intervened to mediate a peace between the two kingdoms'.
wars.note: The Kingdom of Navarre page is silent on Tauste; the García Ramírez page (also the Navarre dossier's source) gives 1146.

certainty.note: No treaty line is on any page opened for the Muslim frontier or for Navarre; counties and conquests are named by town.
The Peace of Támara (1128) 'set the boundary between the two realms', so the Castilian frontier is the one sharp line; the Navarrese frontier after 1134 and the Muslim frontier stay soft.

sources.title: Kingdom of Aragon
sources.note: Infobox: established 1035, capitals Jaca/Huesca 1096/Zaragoza 1118, status independent kingdom 1035-1162, successor Crown of Aragon (1162); Navarre/Aragon split in 1134; Crown created 1150; no area.

sources.title: Alfonso I of Aragon
sources.note: Accession 1104, Urraca 1109, Zaragoza 18 December 1118, Calatayud/Daroca 1120, Soria 1119, Castilian possessions lost 1127, Támara 1128, Fraga 1134, death September 1134. Repair reading: Ejea and Tauste 1105, Valtierra 1106, Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera 1107; Tudela listed without a year.

sources.title: Ramiro I of Aragon
sources.note: 1035 county of Aragon to Ramiro; 1043 annexation of Sobrarbe and Ribagorza; Tafalla and Sangüesa; death at Graus 8 May 1063.

sources.title: Sancho Ramírez
sources.note: King of Aragon 1063, King of Pamplona 1076; Barbastro 1064, Graus 1083, Monzón 1089; died 4 June 1094 at Huesca.

sources.title: Petronilla of Aragon
sources.note: Betrothal 11 August 1137, Ramiro II abdicates 13 November 1137, wedding August 1150; Ramon Berenguer IV princeps.

sources.title: Taifa of Lérida
sources.note: 1100-1101: Aragonese capture Barbastro, Sariñena, Pomar de Cinca and Albalate de Cinca.

sources.title: Battle of Alcoraz
sources.note: 15 November 1096; siege of Huesca from 1094 'nearly two and a half years'; Huesca surrendered less than two weeks later.

sources.title: Peter I of Aragon and Navarre
sources.note: Reign 1094-1104 (death late September); Alcoraz and Huesca given as 1095, Monzón 24 June 1089, Barbastro 1100; marriage at Huesca 16 August 1097.

sources.title: Siege of Barbastro
sources.note: Crusade of August 1064, forty-day siege; Armengol III of Urgel entrusted with the city; retaken 17 April 1065.

sources.title: Urraca of León and Castile
sources.note: Marriage to Alfonso I in October or November 1109; fall 1112 truce and annulment, Alfonso occupying a significant portion of Castile; no town named.

sources.title: Ramiro I de Aragón (es.wikipedia)
sources.note: War with García from 1043, Tafalla 'muy pronto', reconciliation 1044; Sangüesa castle in the alliance of c. 1057; Sobrarbe and Ribagorza 'a partir de 1043' and 'en 1045'.

sources.title: Tudela (Navarra) (es.wikipedia)
sources.note: Reconquered 'definitivamente' by Alfonso I on 25 February 1119, soon after Zaragoza on 18 December 1118.

sources.title: García Ramírez of Navarre
sources.note: 1146: García occupied Tauste, which belonged to Aragon; Alfonso VII mediated a peace.

notes:
IDENTITY. The Kingdom page establishes the kingdom in 1035 and gives its status as independent to 1162, so the dossier runs 1035-1162; Cliopatria's rows run 1015-1168. The Crown of Aragon dossier (another part) starts in 1162 and asks this one to end then; the Crown page and Kingdom page differ on the union (1150 the wedding, 1162 the status change). The infobox states no area, so no area comparison could be made.
CLIOPATRIA. The 1015-1027 row (12 cells) is exactly the County of Pallars Sobirà shape: wrong, not Aragon. Repaired 2026-10-31 after review: the shapes are now drawn in steps that match the ledger. 1040 (8 cells, without the Sangüesa cells) 1035-1042; 1046 without seven cells round Graus, Barbastro and east of Huesca 1043-1075; 1085 without the Huesca cell and those seven 1076-1082; new keyframes 1083 (Graus), 1089 (Monzón), the 1099 shape drawn 1096-1099 as the Huesca conquest (its ten new cells lie west of Huesca, not at Barbastro), new 1100 (Barbastro), 1105 (Ejea, Tauste and the Cinco Villas), 1107 (La Litera); 1111 plus the one cell it drops; 1118 (Ebro valley, Soria, Tudela); 1126 for one year; 1127 without the Castilian possessions; 1139 from 1134. The 1126 shape reaches Burgos, La Rioja, the Basque provinces, Guadalajara and Teruel: the Alfonso I and Urraca pages name none of these places and do not date the acquisition, so the 1126 gain is a bridge (confidence 1).
SETTLED IN THE REPAIR. Peter I reigned 1094-1104 (Peter I page). Huesca fell at the end of November 1096 (Alcoraz page 15 November 1096 plus under two weeks; the Peter I page gives 1095 for the battle and 27 November 1095 for the fall, which the Alcoraz page, the Kingdom page and the Zaragoza dossier contradict). Tudela fell on 25 February 1119 (es.wikipedia Tudela). Barbastro 1064-1065 was a crusader occupation entrusted to Armengol III of Urgel (a contest, not a gain). The Tauste incident of 1146 is on the García Ramírez page, not on the Kingdom of Navarre page.
UNSETTLED. (1) The Castilian possessions: the Urraca page has the marriage in 1109, Urraca's grant of her land in December 1109 and Alfonso 'occupied a significant portion of Castile' in fall 1112, but no town and no later year; the ledger keeps 1126 (confidence 1). (2) Sangüesa: the Ramiro I page (en) has it after Tafalla within 1036-1043; the es.wikipedia page has the war from 1043 and the castle of Sangüesa in c. 1057; 1043 is kept at confidence 1. (3) Soria counterpart is free text because the page names no holder; Ejea, Tauste and La Litera (1105, 1107) are given to the Zaragoza taifa as a reading, and Tudela to the Almoravids as for Calatayud. (4) Mequinenza/Fraga: the page lists them without a capture year. (5) Navarre: the Alfonso I page gives no date for the separation, the Kingdom page 1134. (6) The County of Ribagorza dossier ends in 1045; the Ramiro I pages give 1043 and 1045. (7) Ramiro II's 1134-1137 reign: the Kingdom page gives no regnal list. (8) Petronilla's abdication 18 June 1164 (text) or 18 July 1164 (infobox). (9) Cliopatria's 1111 shape does not reach Sariñena, Pomar de Cinca or Albalate de Cinca.
COUNTERPARTS. 'taifa-of-lerida' has losses of Graus (1083), Monzón (1093, this dossier 1089) and Barbastro (1100); 'taifa-of-zaragoza' has the 1096-11 loss of Huesca but no 1105 or 1107 losses; kingdom-of-navarre records Tauste 1146 against this kingdom.
PAGES. Kingdom of Aragon, Alfonso I of Aragon, Ramiro I of Aragon, Sancho Ramírez, Petronilla of Aragon, Taifa of Lérida (six, one over the budget of five), plus seven pages opened in the repair at the reviewer's request: Battle of Alcoraz, Peter I of Aragon and Navarre, Siege of Barbastro, Urraca of León and Castile, es.wikipedia Ramiro I and Tudela, García Ramírez of Navarre.
GAZETTEER. Huesca (as a place), Sangüesa, Graus, Monzón, Tudela, Calatayud, Barbastro, Tauste, Ejea, Tamarite de Litera are not in places.jsonl; coordinate radii are used.
